title: Bias and variance, aloud
objectives: Explain the bias-variance trade-off with a picture and a finance example.

screens.title: Shrink the estimate
screens.prose: About two minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. An analyst estimates a mean return whose true value is 1. Four years of data with spread 2 give the sample mean $\bar{x}$ a variance of $\sigma^2/n = 4/4 = 1$. She reports $c\bar{x}$ instead.
screens.question: Drag $c$ to the lowest error.

hints.text: Two dashed curves add up to the solid one. Where does the solid curve bottom out?
The bias² curve falls as $c$ rises; the variance curve climbs.
The two dashed curves cross at $c = 0.5$, and the total is lowest there.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the lowest point of the solid curve.

byKey.no-shrink: You left $c$ near 1, the plain mean. Its error is all variance, 1.
byKey.all-shrink: You shrank to 0. That error is all bias, 1.
byKey.p1: Close the gap: the bottom of the solid curve is where both dashed curves meet.

explain.text: Shrinking by $c$ adds bias $(c - 1)$ and scales the variance by $c^2$. The two pull against each other, and the total $(c-1)^2 + c^2$ is lowest at $c = 0.5$.

screens.title: Read the error
screens.prose: Same analyst, same numbers. You have found the best $c$.
screens.question: What is the mean squared error of $0.5\bar{x}$?

hints.text: Add the bias squared and the variance.
The bias of $0.5\bar{x}$ is $0.5 - 1 = -0.5$.
Bias² is 0.25 and the variance is $0.25 \times 1 = 0.25$. Add them.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the bias, then add the variance.

byKey.plain: 1 is the error of $c = 1$ (or of $c = 0$). At $c = 0.5$ it halves.
byKey.bias-only: You squared the bias but left out the variance, $0.25 \times 1$.

explain.text: Bias² is $(0.5 - 1)^2 = 0.25$ and the variance is $0.5^2 \times 1 = 0.25$. Their sum, 0.5, is half the error of the plain mean.

screens.title: Three fits to one sample
screens.prose: Twenty points on $\sin(2\pi x)$ with noise of sd 0.3. Step through polynomial fits of degree 1, 3 and 9. The dashed curve is the truth.

state.caption: Degree 1: training error 0.2542, error against the true curve 0.2049.

frames.caption: Degree 1: training error 0.2542, error against the true curve 0.2049.
Degree 3: training error 0.0499, error against the true curve 0.0115.
Degree 9: training error 0.0378, error against the true curve 0.0205.

screens.question: Which degree is closest to the true curve?

options.why: You picked the lowest training error, 0.0378. Against the truth degree 9 scores 0.0205, worse than 0.0115.
A straight line cannot bend with the sine: its error against the truth is 0.2049.

hints.text: Read the second number in each caption.
Training error is the first number; it always falls with degree.
Against the true curve: 0.2049, 0.0115, 0.0205. Pick the smallest.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the error against the true curve, not the training error.

explain.text: Training error falls from 0.2542 to 0.0499 to 0.0378 as the degree rises. Error against the truth goes 0.2049, 0.0115, 0.0205: it turns back up at degree 9.

canvas.caption: Degree 3: training error 0.0499, error against the true curve 0.0115.

screens.title: Four hundred refits
screens.prose: Now refit each degree on 400 fresh samples and average over a grid (seeded). Bias² is how far the average fit sits from the truth. Variance is how much fits spread. The noise adds 0.09.
screens.question: Fill in the expected test error, bias² + variance + 0.09.

hints.text: Add across each row, then add the noise.
Degree 1 gives 0.3023, degree 3 0.1113, degree 9 0.1310. The rounded parts give one more in the last place.

feedback.correct: Degree 3 wins, 0.1113, as the single fit suggested. The rounded bars sum to 0.3024, 0.1114 and 0.1311.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each row is bias² + variance + 0.09; the noise is in every row.

explain.text: Degree 1 is nearly all bias, degree 9 nearly all variance. Degree 3 balances them and has the lowest test error, 0.1113.

screens.title: The lowest training error
screens.prose: A candidate says: "Degree 9 has the lowest training error, 0.0378, so it is the best model."

state.caption: Degree 9: training error 0.0378, error against the true curve 0.0205.

screens.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: Training error always falls as the model bends more, so it cannot pick the model.
Nothing: the lowest training error is the best model, so degree 9 should win.
options.why: You trusted training error. It rewards fitting the noise in these twenty points.

options.text: Degree 1 is best because it is the simplest, and simple models generalise best.
options.why: Simplest is not best here: its test error, 0.3023, is the worst of the three.

options.text: Degree 9 is right, but it needs more training points before anyone can prove it.
options.why: The 400 refits already show degree 9 is worse, 0.1310 against 0.1113.

hints.text: Which number in the caption is the candidate reading?
Training error falls with every extra degree.
Error against the truth is 0.0205 for degree 9 and 0.0115 for degree 3.

feedback.correct: Training error measures fit to the noise as well as the signal.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what training error rewards.

byKey.agree: That is the trap: the lowest training error is not the lowest test error. Degree 9 chases noise.

explain.text: Training error can only fall as the model gets more flexible. Judge on held-out data: there degree 9 loses to degree 3.

screens.title: Sixteen years of data
screens.prose: Back to the shrunk mean. The analyst now has sixteen years, so the variance of $\bar{x}$ falls from 1 to $4/16 = 0.25$. She keeps $c = 0.5$.
screens.question: What is the error of $0.5\bar{x}$ now?

hints.text: Which part does more data change?
The bias of $0.5\bar{x}$ is still $-0.5$.
Bias² 0.25 plus variance $0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0625$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recompute the variance; keep the bias.

byKey.scaled: You divided the whole error by four. Only the variance falls with more data; the bias² stays 0.25.
byKey.var-only: That is the variance alone. The bias² of 0.25 is still there.
byKey.old: That is the four-year error. The variance part has fallen.

explain.text: More data shrinks the variance, not the bias. With $c$ fixed, the 0.25 of bias² is now most of the error; re-optimising gives $c = 1/1.25 = 0.8$ and error 0.2.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose:
What you found, as the rule:
$$E[(\hat{y} - y)^2] = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \text{noise}$$
Said aloud: "Expected error is bias squared plus variance plus noise. A flexible model has low bias and high variance. The best model sits between, and we find it on held-out data."
screens.question: Put the spoken answer in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Expected error splits into bias squared, variance and noise.
More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance.
So we pick the flexibility that minimises error on held-out data.
So we pick the model with the lowest training error.
lines.why: Training error always falls with flexibility. It cannot find the turning point.

feedback.correct: Rule, then the trade-off, then what you do about it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. State the split, then the trade-off, then the choice.

byKey.d1: You kept the training-error line. That is the trap from earlier.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the answer needs.

explain.text: A good spoken answer names the three terms, says which way each moves, and ends with how you choose. Training error has no place in it.

screens.title: The best shrinkage
screens.prose: Derive the best $c$ for a true mean $\mu$ and $v = \sigma^2/n$. The error of $c\bar{x}$ is $(c - 1)^2\mu^2 + c^2 v$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Write the error: $(c - 1)^2\mu^2 + c^2 v$ (bias² plus variance).
So $c^* = \mu^2/(\mu^2 + v)$, which is 0.5 when $\mu^2 = v = 1$.

lines.why: Unbiased is not least error. The variance term pulls $c^*$ below 1.

hints.text: Start from the error, then use calculus.
The derivative of $(c-1)^2\mu^2$ is $2(c-1)\mu^2$.
Write, differentiate, set to zero, solve.

feedback.correct: $c^* = \mu^2/(\mu^2 + v)$: shrink more when the variance is large.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write the error, differentiate, set to zero, solve.

byKey.x: You kept "unbiased means best". The derivative at $c = 1$ is $2v > 0$, so lowering $c$ helps.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: Setting the derivative to zero gives $c^* = \mu^2/(\mu^2 + v)$. With four years that is $1/2$; with sixteen years, $1/1.25 = 0.8$. The best $c$ needs the true $\mu$, so in practice we pick it on held-out data.

screens.title: A fund's alpha
screens.prose: A fund shows an alpha of about 4% a year over four years. Its excess returns have volatility 8% a year, so the estimate has standard error $8/\sqrt{4} = 4\%$, variance 16 (in %²). Suppose the true alpha is 4%.
screens.question: What is the mean squared error of half the estimate, in %²?

hints.text: This is the hook scaled by 16.
Bias of $0.5\hat\alpha$ is $-2\%$; its variance is $0.25 \times 16$.
Bias² 4 plus variance 4.

feedback.correct: 8 %², half the 16 %² of the raw estimate.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the bias, then add a quarter of the variance.

byKey.plain: That is the raw estimate, $c = 1$: all variance, 16 %².
byKey.bias-only: You counted the bias² of 4 but not the variance of $0.25 \times 16 = 4$.

explain.text: Half the estimate has bias² $(0.5 \times 4)^2 = 4$ and variance $0.25 \times 16 = 4$. Halving the weight halves the error, from 16 to 8.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "What would you do with ten times the data?" Think of the four hundred refits.
screens.question: Which answer would you give?

options.text: Allow a more flexible model: variance is now cheaper, so the best degree moves up.
Keep degree 3: the best degree depends only on the true curve, not on the data.
options.why: The best degree depends on the data size too. Variance falls with $n$; bias does not.

options.text: Use a simpler model: more data brings more noise, so a flexible fit chases more of it.
options.why: Noise per point is the same. More points average it away.

options.text: Nothing changes: bias and variance both fall by ten, so the best degree stays put.
options.why: Only the variance falls with more data, roughly by ten. Bias stays.

hints.text: Which bar shrinks with more data?
Variance falls roughly in proportion to $1/n$.
With variance cheaper, the degree 9 bar of 0.0410 becomes about 0.004.

feedback.correct: Variance is what more data buys down, so flexibility gets cheaper.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which of the two bars depends on $n$.

explain.text: Ten times the data cuts each variance bar by about ten and leaves the bias. In a seeded run on 200 points, degree 9 totals 0.0043 against 0.0062 for degree 3. The optimum moves to a more flexible model.

ideas: Expected squared error is bias² plus variance plus noise.
Flexibility lowers bias and raises variance; held-out error, not training error, finds the balance.
More data lowers the variance, not the bias, so the best model becomes more flexible.
summary.trap: The lowest training error is not the best model: training error always falls with flexibility.

quiz.prose: A true mean of 2, and the sample mean has variance 1. You report $0.5\bar{x}$.
quiz.question: What is its mean squared error?

byKey.mu1: You used a true mean of 1. With 2 the bias doubles.
byKey.bias: That is only the bias². Add the variance 0.25.

explain.text: Bias is $-0.5 \times 2 = -1$, so bias² is 1. The variance is $0.25 \times 1$, giving 1.25; the best $c$ here would be $4/5 = 0.8$.

quiz.prose: A degree 1 fit has bias² 0.2037 and variance 0.0087 over many refits.
quiz.question: What does that say?

options.text: It underfits: almost all the error is bias, so a more flexible model should help.
It overfits: the error is too large, so a simpler model should bring it down.
options.why: Overfitting shows as high variance. Here variance is tiny, 0.0087.

options.text: It needs more data: with ten times the points the error would fall a long way.
options.why: More data lowers variance, which is already small. The bias stays.

options.text: It is the best model, since its variance is lowest and its fits barely move.
options.why: Low variance alone is not enough. Its total error is the largest.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which of the two numbers is large?

explain.text: Bias² is over twenty times the variance. That is a model too rigid for the curve; more flexibility lowers the error.

quiz.prose: A model has bias² 0.02, variance 0.03 and noise variance 0.05.
quiz.question: What is its expected test error?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add all three parts.

byKey.no-noise: You left out the noise, 0.05. It is part of every test error.

explain.text: Expected test error is bias² plus variance plus noise. Here that is 0.10, and no model can get below 0.05.

quiz.prose: You keep $c = 0.5$ for a true mean of 1. The data grow so the variance of $\bar{x}$ goes from 1 towards 0.
quiz.question: What does the error of $0.5\bar{x}$ tend to?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which part of the error does not depend on the data size?

byKey.zero: More data removes the variance, not the bias. A fixed $c = 0.5$ keeps bias² 0.25.

explain.text: Variance $0.25 \times v$ goes to 0 as $v$ falls. The bias $-0.5$ does not, so the error tends to 0.25.
